passage: Arohi here. I was one of eight testers Bhupen invited last Saturday for the language-swap app. The idea: pair two people who each speak what the other wants to learn, for a weekly call. What we got was a sign-up screen and a profile form that crashed twice. No pairing, no call, nothing to try. We spent forty minutes telling Bhupen about the missing "forgot password" link, the tiny letters and a button that did nothing. Not one of us could say whether we would want a partner. Bhupen took notes quickly, smiling, and said, "Great, very helpful." I can't say if that was true. I left with a page of comments about basics and no answer to the only question that mattered.

qa.q: How many testers did Bhupen invite?
qa.a: Arohi was one of eight testers Bhupen invited.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt hearing only comments about basics?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt disappointed or defensive, though the smile and the words "very helpful" hide it, so Arohi cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next to learn whether the idea has value?
qa.a: Bhupen could set up even a simple hand-made pairing and one real call, so testers can try the core idea, and then ask whether they would use it again.

qa.q: How did the testers see the session?
qa.a: The testers, including Arohi, felt they could not judge the idea since there was nothing to try, and left with comments only about basics.

grounding: Shows a founder releasing a version too bare to test the core idea, so feedback is only about missing basics.

Day one. Gautam's idea was a tool that matched home cooks with office workers nearby who wanted lunch. He was so eager to "launch fast" that he built only a sign-up page and a list of cooks' names. No menus, no prices, no way to order.
Day ten. He sent the link to thirty testers. Rukmini, one of them, messaged him: "I signed up. Now what? I can't see what anyone cooks or how to get it."
Day twenty-one. Gautam read all the feedback. Every comment was about missing basics: no menu, no order button, no delivery time. Not one person said whether they liked the idea of home-cooked office lunch. They never got far enough to try it.
He sat back and rubbed his face. Three weeks, and he still didn't know if the idea was any good.

qa.q: How many testers did Gautam send the link to?
qa.a: He sent the link to thirty testers.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt after reading all the feedback?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated and deflated, since three weeks gave him no answer about whether the idea was good.

qa.q: What would you change first in Gautam's first version?
qa.a: Include the one core step, seeing a cook's menu and placing an order, even if roughly done, so testers can actually try the idea.

qa.q: How does Rukmini experience the tool?
qa.a: Rukmini signs up but is left confused, unable to see food or order, so there is nothing to judge.

grounding: It shows a founder releasing a version so bare that testers cannot try the core idea, so feedback is only about missing basics.

passage:
Vaibhav, you say your first version is "just a landing page". Let your Chetan Chacha tell you about my furniture-rental idea when I was twenty-five.
I wanted to rent furniture to students who move every year. I was told, start small. So I made a website with our name, a nice photo of a sofa, and a button that said "Coming soon, leave your email."
Two hundred people left their emails. I was thrilled. Then I asked them for feedback. Everyone said the same thing: what does it cost, what can I rent, how long, who delivers?
I had learned nothing about whether students actually wanted to rent. I'd only learned that people will type an email into a box.
Next time, I rented out five real beds to five real students for one month. That taught me more in four weeks than that website did in four months.

qa.q: How many people left their emails?
qa.a: Two hundred people left their emails.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel when two hundred emails came in?
qa.a: Chetan felt thrilled at first, though later he realised it had taught him nothing about the real idea.

qa.q: At the point he built the website, what else could Chetan have done, and why?
qa.a: He could have rented a few real pieces to a few students, as he did later, because that tests the core idea directly.

qa.q: How might the students who left emails have felt about the site?
qa.a: They were probably curious but confused, with no prices or details, which is why their feedback was only about basics.

grounding: It shows a founder whose first version is so bare that people cannot try the core idea, so feedback is about missing basics, not the idea's value.
